4.2 Mean–Variance Portfolio Theory

Portfolios of two assets

Section titled “Portfolios of two assets”

0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance showed how the variance of a two-asset portfolio depends on the correlation. Now draw each portfolio on one chart, with standard deviation on the horizontal axis and expected return on the vertical axis. Let assets A and B have expected returns μA\mu_AμA​ and μB\mu_BμB​, standard deviations σA\sigma_AσA​ and σB\sigma_BσB​, and correlation ρ\rhoρ, and let the weight of A be www:

μp=wμA+(1−w)μB,σp2=w2σA2+(1−w)2σB2+2w(1−w)ρσAσB\mu_p = w\mu_A + (1 - w)\mu_B, \qquad \sigma_p^2 = w^2\sigma_A^2 + (1 - w)^2\sigma_B^2 + 2w(1 - w)\rho\sigma_A\sigma_Bμp​=wμA​+(1−w)μB​,σp2​=w2σA2​+(1−w)2σB2​+2w(1−w)ρσA​σB​

The expected return is a weighted average of the two and changes in a straight line with www; the standard deviation does not (portfolio variance). As www goes from 0 to 1, the portfolio traces a curve on the chart. With w<0w < 0w<0 or w>1w > 1w>1 one asset is sold short (short selling), and the curve extends at both ends.

Check C1
In Figure 1-1, change the correlation from 0.2 to −1. How does the curve of portfolios change?
Which correlation gives the straight line joining A and B? Try ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1 in the figure.
When the correlation falls, more of the two assets' swings cancel out. Does portfolio risk rise or fall?
Which term of the portfolio variance formula contains ρ\rhoρ?

Of all possible portfolios, the one with the lowest variance is the minimum-variance portfolio. With two assets, its weight can be found with a derivative (Exercises Question 1).

Check C2
A has an expected return of 10% and a standard deviation of 20%; B has 5% and 10%; their correlation is 0.2. What does the minimum-variance portfolio look like?
Starting from everything in B, add a little A. How does the portfolio variance change? With a correlation of only 0.2, part of A's swings is offset by B.
Set the weight of A to 0.5 in the figure and compare the standard deviation with that of everything in B.
A's standard deviation is twice B's. Would the lowest-variance portfolio put most of the money in the riskier asset?

The efficient frontier

Section titled “The efficient frontier”

With more than two assets, the possible portfolios fill a region of the chart. For each target expected return mmm, find the portfolio with the lowest variance; the curve these portfolios form is the minimum-variance frontier. Its leftmost point is the minimum-variance portfolio.

The half of the frontier below the minimum-variance portfolio is of no use: at the same standard deviation, the portfolios on the upper half have higher expected returns. The part of the minimum-variance frontier above the minimum-variance portfolio is the efficient frontier: the highest expected return for the risk, and the lowest risk for the expected return.

Finding portfolios on the frontier is a constrained optimization problem. Suppose there are NNN assets with weights wiw_iwi​ and expected returns μi\mu_iμi​, and let σij\sigma_{ij}σij​ be the covariance of assets iii and jjj (σii=σi2\sigma_{ii} = \sigma_i^2σii​=σi2​). The portfolio’s variance is

σp2=∑i=1N∑j=1Nwiwjσij\sigma_p^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_i w_j \sigma_{ij}σp2​=i=1∑N​j=1∑N​wi​wj​σij​

It is minimized subject to two constraints:

∑i=1Nwiμi=m,∑i=1Nwi=1\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \mu_i = m, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i = 1i=1∑N​wi​μi​=m,i=1∑N​wi​=1

This is the mean–variance optimization proposed by Markowitz (1952). Each constraint has its own Lagrange multiplier (Lagrange multiplier); setting the partial derivative with respect to each wiw_iwi​ to 0 gives the weights on the frontier (Exercises Question 2).

Check C3
Among investors who care only about expected return and variance, those with different degrees of risk aversion choose different portfolios on the efficient frontier, but none chooses a portfolio below the efficient frontier.
Think: compare a portfolio below the efficient frontier with the frontier portfolio directly above it. How do their risk and expected return compare?

Short-sale constraints

Section titled “Short-sale constraints”

Many investors (such as most mutual funds and individual retirement accounts) cannot sell short. Then the constraint wi≥0w_i \ge 0wi​≥0 is added; this is a short-sale constraint. With it, the optimum may lie on the boundary, with some weights exactly 0; this is the same kind of problem as the corner solutions of 0.2 Optimization: at the optimum, the tangency condition no longer holds.

Check C4
After adding a short-sale constraint, the efficient frontier:
After adding a constraint, are there more portfolios to choose from, or fewer?
If a frontier portfolio needs a short sale without the constraint, can it still be chosen with the constraint?
Portfolios without short sales (such as everything in one asset) can still be chosen, so the optimization still has a solution.

What diversification does

Section titled “What diversification does”

The benefit of diversification comes from correlations below 1. Adding a new asset to the choices cannot make the efficient frontier worse: every old portfolio is still available (with a weight of 0 on the new asset). When can the new asset make the frontier better?

Check C5
An asset has a lower expected return than every existing asset. Adding it to the choices cannot make the efficient frontier better.
Think: if this asset has a very low or even negative correlation with the others, how would adding a little of it affect portfolio risk?

The benefit of diversification also shows up in long-run compound growth. 4.1 Measuring Return and Risk showed that volatility drags down compound growth; by lowering volatility, diversification can raise compound growth even without raising the expected return (Exercises Question 4).

Limits of the method

Section titled “Limits of the method”

Mean–variance optimization gives a clear framework, but using it in practice raises several problems:

  • The inputs must be estimated. Estimates of expected returns have large errors (4.1 Measuring Return and Risk), and the optimizer “believes” them, putting large amounts in assets whose estimates are too high and often producing extreme weights (Exercises Question 3). 4.10 Estimation Error and Robust Optimization is devoted to this problem.
  • Variance treats rises and falls alike and ignores fat tails and maximum drawdown.
  • It is a single-period model that ignores the investor’s horizon, income and liabilities.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Two-asset portfolios: the expected return changes in a straight line with the weight, the standard deviation does not; the lower the correlation, the more the curve bends to the left.
  • The minimum-variance portfolio has the lowest variance; the minimum-variance frontier holds the lowest-variance portfolio for each target expected return; the efficient frontier is its part above the minimum-variance portfolio.
  • Mean–variance optimization: minimize σp2\sigma_p^2σp2​ subject to ∑wiμi=m\sum w_i \mu_i = m∑wi​μi​=m and ∑wi=1\sum w_i = 1∑wi​=1, solvable with Lagrange multipliers.
  • A short-sale constraint wi≥0w_i \ge 0wi​≥0 may put the optimum on the boundary.
  • Adding a new asset cannot make the efficient frontier worse; diversification can also raise compound growth.
  • Estimation errors in the inputs make optimization results very unstable.
